item.base_system: CrMnFeCoNi equiatomic high-entropy alloy (20 at.% each)
item.intervention: Heating in a vacuum environment (4.2 × 10⁻⁶ atm) from room temperature to 1100 °C
item.processing: In situ High Temperature X-ray Diffraction (HTXRD) with heating rate of 15 °C/min, holding 5 min at set points, CuKα radiation
item.test_conditions: Vacuum pressure ~4.2 × 10⁻⁶ atm, temperature range 25 °C to 1100 °C
item.structure_change: Formation of MnO (halite-type) oxide starting at 700 °C; substrate FCC phase remained stable; no Cr₂O₃, Fe₂O₃, or Fe₃O₄ observed
item.property_change: Formation of a thin oxide layer (>0.5 μm) with sugar-like granules; Mn depletion in the near-surface region
item.attributed_mechanism: Lower oxygen partial pressure favors MnO formation; Mn has high affinity for oxygen and high vapor pressure, consuming available oxygen
quotes: In a vacuum (4.2 × 10⁻⁶ atm), only MnO, a halite-type oxide, was formed during in situ oxidation
The new peaks during phase identification were found to be MnO, and the substrate material conserved its phase stability throughout up to 1100 °C
The analysis of the oxide-formed layer revealed the formation of MnO having a cubic crystal structure of lattice parameter 4.510 Å

item.intervention: Comparison of oxidation products between vacuum and air environments
item.processing: In situ HTXRD analysis followed by SEM-EDS characterization of oxidized surfaces
item.test_conditions: Vacuum (4.2 × 10⁻⁶ atm) vs. Air (1.0 atm), up to 1100 °C
item.structure_change: Vacuum: MnO only; Air: Mn₂O₃, Mn₃O₄, MnCr₂O₄, Fe₃Mn₃O₈; No Cr₂O₃ or Fe₂O₃ in either environment
item.property_change: Oxide scale in air is thicker (up to 3.45 μm) and darker (dark brown) compared to vacuum (thin, greenish, <0.5 μm)
item.attributed_mechanism: Oxygen partial pressure dictates oxide type; higher pressure leads to mixed spinel oxides and Mn₃O₄ formation
quotes: The thickness of the oxide layer formed in a vacuum is smaller than that formed in air using HTXRD
The colour of the sample was dark brown compared to one in the vacuum with a whitish oxide surface

item.intervention: Thermodynamic calculation using ThermoCalc (CALPHAD method) for oxide formation
item.processing: Equilibrium calculations using TCS Ni-based Superalloys Database (TCNi12) varying oxygen partial pressure from 1×10⁻¹⁴ to 1.0 atm
item.structure_change: Prediction: Spinel oxides at atmospheric pressure; Halite oxides (NiO, CoO) at low pressure; MnO predicted at very low pressure
item.property_change: Discrepancy: ThermoCalc predicted NiO and CoO halites in vacuum, but experiment showed only MnO; ThermoCalc predicted spinel in air, experiment showed mixed spinels including Mn₃O₄
item.attributed_mechanism: Discrepancies attributed to time scale; thermodynamic calculations assume equilibrium, while experiments are kinetic; MnO formation favored by more negative Gibbs free energy
quotes: ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results
ThermoCalc predicts NiO as the major halite oxide type even at the same equilibrium temperature (700 °C) at which the initial oxide MnO formed during an experiment in a vacuum
Such a discrepancy in results between the ThermoCalc-predicted oxide types (i.e., NiO, CoO) and the experimentally found one (MnO only) could be the time scale

item.intervention: Annealing at 900 °C for 48 h followed by cold rolling to 1.6 mm thickness
item.processing: Arc melting, drop casting, electromagnetic stirring, annealing, cold rolling
item.structure_change: Coarse equiaxed grain structure (up to 0.1 mm) with annealing twins; single-phase FCC solid solution; no sigma phase or segregation
item.property_change: Homogeneous elemental distribution; presence of casting porosity and oxide inclusions (MnCr₂O₄ type)
item.attributed_mechanism: Homogenization at elevated temperature results in single-phase solid solution; inclusions are likely pre-existing oxides
quotes: The cast alloy was re-melted multiple times and, for thorough mixing of the elements, highly effective electromagnetic stirring was used to promote homogeneity

item.intervention: Exposure to high temperature in air leading to Mn depletion
item.processing: In situ HTXRD oxidation followed by EDS mapping
item.structure_change: Mn-depleted zone visible in EDS map; stratified oxide layer with Mn-rich top and Cr-rich inner layer
item.property_change: Depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy beneath the oxide layer; formation of non-protective oxides
item.attributed_mechanism: Mn has the highest diffusion rate and vapor pressure, leading to preferential outward diffusion and oxidation

item.intervention: Thermodynamic calculation of phase stability vs. temperature
item.processing: CALPHAD method using ThermoCalc to generate one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions
item.test_conditions: Temperature range from room temperature to 1320 °C
item.structure_change: Single-phase FCC region stable from 750 °C to 1320 °C; sigma phase forms below 585 °C; BCC phase forms at 500 °C
item.property_change: Thermal stability restricted to 750–1320 °C for single-phase FCC; decomposition at lower temperatures
item.attributed_mechanism: Thermodynamic calculations restrict thermal stability; lower temperature decomposition products like sigma phase form due to equilibrium conditions
quotes: From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA's single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C
One lower temperature phase is the sigma phase that formed below 585 °C and remained stable in temperatures down to 205 °C
CALPHAD predictions provide information on the phase equilibria at the heat treatment temperature, as well as the solvus and equilibrium solidus temperatures

item.intervention: Thermodynamic calculation of oxide formation vs. oxygen partial pressure
item.processing: ThermoCalc with TCS Ni-based Superalloys Database
item.test_conditions: Oxygen partial pressure from 1×10⁻¹⁴ to 1.0 atm at 1000 °C
item.structure_change: Spinel oxides dominant at 1 atm; Halite oxides (NiO, CoO) predicted at low pressure; MnO dominant at very low pressure
item.property_change: Predicted transition from spinel to halite oxides as pressure drops below 3.42 × 10⁻² atm

item.intervention: Comparison of oxidation products with previous literature
item.processing: Review of cited studies on isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi
item.test_conditions: Various temperatures and atmospheres from literature
item.structure_change: Contradiction: Previous studies reported Cr₂O₃, Fe₂O₃, Fe₃O₄; this study found none
item.property_change: This study found only Mn-based oxides (MnO, Mn₂O₃, Mn₃O₄) and mixed spinels (MnCr₂O₄, Fe₃Mn₃O₈)
item.attributed_mechanism: In situ technique reveals real-time phase formation; previous post-mortem analyses may have missed transient phases or assumed equilibrium
quotes: The list of oxides that were identified is different from most of the studies that analysed the high-temperature isothermal oxidation resistance of CrMnFeCoNi alloy
